paragraphs: Two signboards hung over Baishi’s south gate, the old one above the new. Rain had soaked the five characters “Great Jin Baishi Garrison” almost black. The lower board, “Great Qin Baishi County Office,” had been hung only a year ago; its yellow timber still gave off a clean, fresh scent. The authorities had tried several times to remove one or the other, but before a man could climb the ladder, crowds would gather in the city. In the end no one touched either board.

Two lanes in the city shared a single well. The southern half of its stone curb bore the names of those who had repaired it under Jin; the northern side had acquired an additional row of dates when Qin troops dredged the canal. The neighborhood headman forbade soldiers to interfere with the well, yet a newly arrived garrison man, seeing the rope worn through, offered to replace it with hemp cord from the camp. Elders on either side argued over which knot would spare the wooden windlass, nearly bringing a dispute about a well rope before the magistrate. In the end the soldier laid the new rope alongside the old and told everyone to draw water first.

Guo Cheng, on the eastern side of town, had a Qin registration tablet nailed to his door. The year before, when Huan Xuan’s soldiers passed through and the town had no grain, he had carried his sick daughter from place to place begging for food. It was Qin grain from the northern bank that saved his family. Officials then allotted him twelve mu of uncultivated land under the new register. But the field’s former owner, Zhao Hong’an, still lived in the western ward, with the ancestral title deed in a camphorwood chest. He took it out to air whenever he made offerings to his ancestors.

Gu Qian of the western ward had served as a county assistant magistrate under Jin. He fled when Huan Xuan entered Jiankang. Now he had put on his mold-spotted official robe again and spent day and night urging the city to welcome Jin rule. At the wharf, Sun Liu carried both Qin and Jin permits. Qin soldiers demanded the former when inspecting salt; southerners demanded the latter when examining cloth. The seals of two states could save his boat—or keep it motionless at a ferry for a whole day.

On the seventh day after Murong Chui was buried, cavalry raised dust outside the south gate. He Wuji arrived with two hundred Beifu soldiers and an edict from the Jin emperor demanding the return of Baishi, Qinglin, and Shiliang. From the battlements Qin commander Du Heng listened to the edict being read aloud, then asked whether it contained any provision for people who had received land, served in the army, or entered household registers while Qin held the city. He Wuji answered that Beifu military orders forbade reprisals against those formerly registered under Qin, and that families wishing to go north would be allowed to do so.
“Can they carry their fields away on their backs?” Du Heng asked.
He Wuji stood before his horse with the scroll in his hand. “Land rights will be checked separately. We cannot leave the walls in your hands until the land claims have all been settled.”

Du Heng did not reject the edict. He requested three days for deliberation and asked the Beifu Army to stay five li from the gates in the meantime. He Wuji would not withdraw that far. He established a camp in the southern outskirts and sent word to the commanders at Qinglin and Shiliang. Before dark, spectators had crowded Baishi’s south gate so thoroughly that no carts could pass. Everyone knew an answer would come in three days. No one knew whether the gate would still open as usual afterward.

A long table was carried into the county office courtyard. Gu Qian sat on the eastern side, with Zhao Hong’an and several established families beside him. Guo Cheng stood below the steps holding an allotment voucher worn soft by sweat. Wives of military households squeezed into the crowd with children in their hands. Gu Qian declared that Baishi was Jin territory and the restoration of Jin must naturally restore its former officials and laws. Guo Cheng asked where the seal of the Jin government had been hiding when people starved in the streets. Gu Qian flushed red and answered only that a temporary loss in troubled times could not extinguish a frontier held for a hundred years. Zhao Hong’an presented his old deed. Without yet arguing with the military families, he first demanded that the county clerk publicly acknowledge the authenticity of its official seal. The clerk recognized that seal, and also the different one on the Qin land register. He dared not simply nod.
“Last year you lived in a ruined hut outside my estate,” Zhao Hong’an finally said to Guo Cheng. “Even your seed grain was borrowed from my family.”

“Master Zhao remembers the seed,” Guo Cheng answered, “but it was Qin soldiers who brought medicine for my daughter. I have the debt for seed written down. When the winter harvest comes, you can collect it. But my hoe has left its marks in those twelve mu. One old deed cannot erase the year I spent working them.”

Sun Liu squatted under the veranda and listened until the county clerk asked him to speak for the traders. Yesterday, he said, three of his salt boats had been searched separately by the two armies; the men hired to unload them had gone home. If trade was still blocked tomorrow, people in the city would be scraping their old pickling jars for salt. Gu Qian rebuked him for knowing nothing of the dignity of the state. Sun Liu bowed and said he knew only this: taxes still had to be paid, boats still had to be rowed, and those who defended the dignity of a state still had to eat salt.

At the far end of the table, others made way for a white-haired man called Old Tian. His grandson served in the Jin army, his son-in-law had driven carts for Qin, and he himself held three documents: a Jin household registration, a Qin guest-household registration, and a replacement land voucher. He pressed all three to his chest and asked Gu Qian whether, if the city went back to Jin, his grandson could still visit him, and whether his son-in-law would henceforth have to hide. His questions came out tangled. Two young clerks bent over their ledgers together, paging through every county register on the table without finding a precedent that could explain all three papers at once.

The first day’s debate ran past midnight. It resumed the next day, with the clamor outside the county office louder than a market. Du Heng recorded every household’s statement in three columns—land, service, and registration—and ordered the clerks to make two copies for comparison with the Jin envoy on the third day. During the night someone tried to hang a Jin banner from the city tower and was driven back by the guards. Military families posted notices saying that if Qin withdrew, they would move north with everyone in their households. Baishi’s gates remained open, but the number of boats at the wharf fell by half.

On the third morning, with the mist still hanging low, He Wuji came south of the city with twelve attendants. Du Heng withdrew the heavy crossbows from the gate and descended the walls in person. The two sides spread their papers across a long table, with Old Tian, Sun Liu, and others permitted to observe. He Wuji announced that land cultivated since the previous year would not be reassigned for the present. Jin troops would not treat receipt of Qin grain, change to Qin household registration, or service hauling supplies for Qin as a crime. Those who wished to migrate north might take their property; officials of both states would examine disputed land prices. Criminal cases and old debts would be registered together, and no commander might settle them privately.

The terms were gentler than the rumors of the previous two days, and Guo Cheng breathed a little more easily. Still, he asked which magistrate he should obey when next year’s planting began, if his allotment remained only provisionally protected. Du Heng asked whether Jin would allow Qin officials to participate in the review of old cases for three years. He Wuji replied that once the city belonged to Jin it must obey Jin officers; Qin officials could bring evidence and challenge claims, but could not establish a second government office inside the walls. Du Heng said the existing Qin-registered households needed something they could rely on, and the two states must still agree on the sequence of garrison withdrawal. The tone of the meeting, warm for a moment, turned cold again.

Outside, someone carrying a Jin banner pushed toward the gate. The banner had been brought by a former subordinate of Gu Qian, who meant to hoist it after the negotiations. Several youths, however, could not wait and began climbing the wooden rails to plant it at once. Military families registered under Qin mistook the movement for an attempt by Jin troops to seize the gate and rushed forward to stop them. Those behind saw only the scuffle and feared the gate was about to close, so pressed forward harder. A girl fell beside a horse’s hooves. Her mother cried out. Many turned at the sound; more kept pushing.

On the city wall, a Qin crossbowman had been ordered to put his weapon back on its rack. As he turned, its stock swung south. A young officer beside He Wuji, Shen Cheng, saw the movement and thought the weapon had been aimed at his commander. He shouted for the guards. He Wuji was raising his hand to keep everyone calm, but Shen Cheng snatched up a bow and loosed the first arrow. Du Heng ducked at the sound of the string. The shaft grazed his helmet and struck the neck of a banner bearer behind him. The man sank to his knees against the wall, and half the Qin banner fell into the crowd.
A cry went up from the battlements: “Jin troops have shot a man!”

Some men leveled crossbows; others tried to wrench them away. The first bolt missed everyone and buried itself beside a leg of the negotiating table. The second passed through the land registers, nailing the pages to the wood. The third flew into the crowd. Du Heng drew his sword and ran toward the gate, shouting all the while for crossbows to be lowered. He Wuji spun around, kicked Shen Cheng to the ground, and took his sword, but already soldiers of both armies were surging forward from opposite sides.

Someone carried the girl over the overturned table, her clothes thick with mud and blood. Old Tian bent to protect the three papers held against his chest. A stray arrow struck beneath his ribs. He looked down; his knees hit the table, and he fell with his documents into the rain-soaked land registers.

Inside the gate, Du Heng struck a soldier’s spear apart with his sword and ordered him back into formation. The man had just seen a comrade fall. His eyes were red, and he shouted for vengeance. Du Heng struck his shoulder with the flat of his blade, almost driving him to his knees. “Do you still know your unit number? Back!” On the other side, He Wuji personally led shield troops between the stampeding groups and forbade them to pursue the enemy into the city. Both armies had wounded and dead. Arrows were still flying, yet the shouts of commanders trying to stop the violence began to drown out the cries to kill. In less than a quarter of an hour, more than a dozen bodies lay on the ground, with many more injured.

The first military report counted twenty-seven dead: nine Qin soldiers, six Jin soldiers, and twelve civilians. Later the county office sent another list of the gravely wounded. Some names on the first list had been mistakenly recorded as dead, while others who died overnight had not been included. Sun Liu personally led men to identify the bodies. He recognized the girl’s mother and Old Tian, but not several of the soldiers.

Each army came to collect its comrades; no one at first came for the civilian dead. Sun Liu took the door planks off his shop and ordered his assistants and boatmen from the northern bank to carry them away together. Old Tian’s hand still clutched papers stuck to one another by blood. Sun Liu did not force the fingers apart. He merely folded the old man’s hands across his chest.

The Qin and Jin camps gathered their dead separately. Du Heng ordered the city shut, but forbade his soldiers to shoot at retreating men. He opened the granaries to families of civilians killed or wounded, requiring both merchants and county clerks to verify the names of those claiming relief. Gu Qian, injured and still wearing his old official robe, insisted that the Jin banner be raised. Du Heng told him to identify the wounded first. Gu Qian looked at him, and at last argued no more. Guo Cheng took the Qin registration tablet down from his door. His wife, startled, asked whether he meant to defect to Jin. He wrapped the wooden tablet and his old Jin household voucher together and put them beneath the stove, unwilling to burn either.

He Wuji had Shen Cheng brought under guard to his command tent. He asked, one detail at a time, where the guards had stood, which way the crossbow had turned, and where the arrow had come from. He ordered Shen Cheng to identify his own bow. Shen Cheng admitted that he had fired first, but still maintained that he was protecting his commander and could not wait for a bolt from the walls. Had he heard an order to shoot? No. Had he actually seen Qin soldiers fire first? After a long time looking at the ground, he said only that the mist had been thick and he could not be certain.

Under military law, unauthorized commencement of missile fire that harmed civilians carried the death penalty. Shen Cheng lay prostrate in the tent, his face pale, and asked to write a final letter to his mother back home. He Wuji allowed it. The letter was sealed in the army’s dispatch bag, and Shen Cheng was executed at dawn the following day. Several Beifu veterans pleaded for a reprieve, arguing that the first arrow had been loosed in confusion, that northern crossbows had also wounded people, and that Jin should not bear the disgrace alone. He Wuji entered the first shot on the first line of his report and made his deputy read it before sealing the document. Executing one guilty man could not make amends for every death; concealing the truth could not answer for even one of them.

When the report reached the southern camp, Liu Yu first examined the names of the dead and wounded. He asked whether the families of the civilians killed had received wooden passes recognized by both states. He Wuji said the matter was still under negotiation. Liu Yu immediately ordered a clerk to send another letter requesting joint identification of bodies, mutual recognition of the injured, and permission for relatives to cross the warning line to claim their dead. He also ordered Shen Cheng’s unauthorized shot and punishment under military law to be described in full. Qin officials could copy the account if they wished; his own men were not to erase the first arrow.

Only then did he study the map of the three cities. Two navigable channels ran from Baishi to Qinglin, while Shiliang controlled a ferry farther upstream. Several officers argued that, since their own side had first broken faith, they should halt any advance until Qin replied. Liu Yu shook his head. Having sent Shen Cheng to military justice, he said, they must bear responsibility for that first arrow. But if Qin soldiers entered a city under the pretext of protecting grain and then refused forever to leave, the dispute over the three cities would remain. He ordered He Wuji to hold the southern road, send more naval patrols to reconnoiter, and keep every man away from the gate without direct orders. Any soldier taking grain privately would be executed on the spot. No street youths were to rush ahead and plant Jin banners.
“So we neither withdraw nor attack?” Liu Yi asked.

“Hold the line of march,” Liu Yu replied. “First let those in the cities who want to move north go out, and receive those who wish to return to Jin registration. If Qin agrees, we can save the living before anything else. If it refuses, we will discuss our next move.”

Some officers complained that this was a sign of weakness. Liu Yu took one of them behind the camp to see the wounded. A Jin archer’s left arm had been severed, and his wife was stitching a torn sleeve beside him. Nearby lay the younger brother of a Qin banner bearer, secretly brought out by townspeople in search of medical help. Young Jin soldiers had wanted to drive the Qin boy away. Liu Yu ordered a physician to dress his wounds, a clerk to record his name, and arrangements for his return when both sides agreed. The young Qin soldier asked which state would pay for his medicine. Liu Yu answered, “Put it on my account for now.”

On the northern bank, Fu Jian received Du Heng’s report while studying the maps left by Murong Chui. One of the river mouths circled in vermilion lay by Baishi. Beside it was a line of tiny writing: “A city can be held; its people’s hearts are harder to take.” Fu Jian laid out three casualty lists. One gave twenty-seven dead, another thirty-four, and the third no fewer than forty-one, having counted seven severely wounded men still alive among the dead. He ordered Fu Rong to send other army officials to verify the names with local merchants, Qin and Jin alike, and to begin by writing the victims' family names correctly.

Zhu Xu was summoned as well. Since returning south he had gone back and forth across the frontier; today he still wore his old Jin robe and carried no Qin official seal at his belt. The three cities, he said, had belonged to Jin, but Qin troops had genuinely saved lives after entering them. If Jin retook them only to punish everyone who had received Qin grain, the south would never again win trust. If Qin used that assistance to hold the cities forever, the south would never again dare open its gates to request help.

Fu Rong asked whether someone must not eventually withdraw, or were both armies to remain outside the walls? Zhu Xu looked at the two sets of household registrations on the table and paused. “Perhaps we should begin by asking the people inside the cities. It is easy to ask which state they belong to. Ask who will cultivate their fields and who will collect next year’s taxes, and only then will you learn what matters to them.”

Fu Jian remembered the petition from the woman aboard the salt boat. He and Liu Yu had pledged in writing that civilian vessels could pass and earlier registrations were not crimes. Only days later, bodies lay before Baishi’s gate, separately claimed by the names of his own state and the state across the river.

Fu Jian ordered fresh copies of the two-state agreement sent to Du Heng for public reading. If an officer or soldier used that single arrow as a pretext to retaliate against civilian households, his commander would share the guilt. Qin might reinforce its existing defensive positions but could not cross the boundary or requisition fields and grain from the city as war expenses. Anyone registered under Qin who wished to migrate north was to receive the proper guest-household vouchers at government granaries along the road; those who wished to remain registered under Jin were not to be secretly detained.
“And if Jin troops insist on entering the city by force?” Fu Rong asked.
“Hold it,” Fu Jian said.

It was the only word he spoke that night that sounded like the Heavenly King of former days. The commanders received the order and went out to arrange their forces. Yet Fu Jian called Fu Rong back and pointed to the tiny characters on the map. He was to inspect in person whether the reinforcement route passed through inhabited villages. If passage was necessary, the villages must be warned in advance and crops compensated by the mu. The strokes Murong Chui had left behind were crooked, as if dragged by a hand trembling with illness; every instruction was still of use.

The southern bank was assembling troops at the same time. Liu Yu issued orders to former officials of the three cities: fields redistributed after Qin entered were to remain with their current cultivators for one year. Former owners with deeds must submit them for official examination; they could not march in with private retainers to seize land. Changes of registration and previous grain-transport service would not be treated as private offenses.

When the draft order reached Jiankang, several great old families objected that ancestral property could not be suspended by military decree. Liu Yu sent back two sentences: let them first identify and release the tenant families they had hidden during the war, then they could discuss the return of their former estates. Southern scholars denounced his roughness when the reply became known. In the three cities, however, many military households cultivating disputed fields quietly asked whether promises made by Jin soldiers could truly be relied on.

Qin reinforcements came down the northern road to Baishi and pitched camp before approaching the gate. To the south, Beifu warships anchored at the new river mouth, flying their military banners but shooting no arrows. Under the earlier agreement merchant boats should have been free to travel, but with two armies inspecting them, boatmen were still queuing at sunset. A boat-owning family fleeing with wife and children was held in midstream: the southern bank demanded Jin documents, the northern bank a Qin guest-household registration. The children cried through the night in the cabin. Sun Liu knew the owner and rowed out to plead for him. Only at midnight did he obtain a wooden pass accepted on both banks.
As Sun Liu handed the pass into the cabin, the owner asked, “Shopkeeper Sun, will it still be good tomorrow morning?”
Sun Liu gazed at the dense camp lights on either side. “That depends on whether the guards recognize it tomorrow.”

Several days later, Baishi still displayed both signboards. Former Jin officials debated seals outside the south gate; the Qin county office audited grain at the northern granary. Each army added another layer of barricades at its end of the bridge, and neither dared be first to cross the water. Old Tian’s grandson finally came over from the Jin camp, and his son-in-law obtained half a day’s leave from the Qin grain convoy. Together they buried a wooden marker over the old man’s grave in a patch of wasteland. Neither wrote the name of a state. As they finished, the grandson drew out a crumpled sheet and asked whether it was the land voucher his grandfather had always carried. The son-in-law said it was, folded it carefully, and wedged it into a crack in the stone before the grave, leaving wind and rain to soak it slowly.

Before departing, the grandson submitted a petition at each of the two county offices, asking who had first turned a crossbow toward the bridge. The Qin clerk told him to obtain the Jin army’s account first; the Jin clerk said he must wait for Qin to examine the arrows. The young man tucked both receipts away without tearing up either. His grandfather had died protecting three title documents. Now the young man too possessed three papers, but none yet disclosed which arrow had killed anyone.

West of the city the wheat had turned yellow. Fearing the passage of two armies, farmers cut the half-ripe ears by night. Among the reeds, every time a Jin sentry detail changed, the Qin troops altered their watch-fire signals in response. Someone mistook the sound of an axe across the water for the dismantling of a bridge. Archers hurried onto the lookout tower, only to learn from the returning patrol that fishermen had been repairing a boat. Word reached the commanders' tents on both banks. No one dared ridicule the alarmed sentry.

On the northern bank, Fu Jian approved his final order for battle preparations: if attacked, each unit was to protect granaries, vessels, and noncombatants in the cities first. Those entering villages to seize people in violation of orders would be punished under military law. To the south, Liu Yu put away the transit tokens and each unit’s grain figures, instructing He Wuji not to squander the entire river fleet merely to retake one city. The two orders went out along the river at nearly the same time. Hooves struck the damp embankments, their sound swallowed by the mist.

No one else died in Baishi that day. But along the upper and lower Fei River, men were already measuring granary ditches, testing bridge foundations, and sounding the depth of ferry crossings. On a merchant boat, an old helmsman heard that both Qin and Jin permitted civilian craft to sail as usual. He nonetheless hid a bundle of dry reeds beneath the deck and told his son that if armed soldiers came at night to requisition their boat, he should first ask whether they would leave their names. “Soldiers in wartime will never give their names,” the son said. “Then do not lend it,” the old man replied.

After dark, the river seemed to narrow as more fires appeared along its banks. Beifu skiffs lay hidden among the reeds; Qin grain wagons moved one by one along the northern dike. The first north wind stirred the wheat left standing, and the wooden marker at Old Tian’s grave quivered. The seals of three cities were still being contested. The dead were already in the ground. Patrols on both banks took roll call as usual and wrote, ‘No fighting tonight.’ Whether they could write the same words tomorrow, no one would say.
